narration: Imagine falling asleep... and finding yourself in a world where donkeys have butterfly wings, roosters have bull horns, and lions have the heads of eagles. And all of them are shouting one strange word at you: "Alebrijes! Alebrijes!" Sounds like a wild dream, right? Well... it was. And that dream changed Mexican art forever. Today, we're uncovering the true story of the alebrijes.

title: What is an alebrije?
narration: First things first: what is an alebrije? Alebrijes are brightly colored sculptures of fantastic creatures, usually mixing parts of two or more real animals. Think of a jaguar with wings, a fish with lizard legs, or a dragon covered in dots, stripes, and swirls in every color you can imagine. Today you can find them all over Mexico, and all over the world. But here's the surprising part: they're young! Alebrijes were born less than one hundred years ago, in Mexico City.

title: Pedro Linares López (1906–1992)
narration: Meet Pedro Linares López. He was born in Mexico City in 1906, and he was a cartonero: an artist who builds figures out of paper and cardboard. Pedro made piñatas, masks, and giant papier-mâché figures called Judas, which were traditionally burned in noisy, fiery celebrations during Holy Week. He learned the craft from his family, and his hands were always busy with paper, paste, and paint.

title: 1936: A dangerous fever
narration: But in 1936, when Pedro was about thirty years old, he became seriously ill. He had a terrible fever, and he fell into a deep sleep. It was so deep that his family worried he might never wake up. And while his body lay in bed... his mind traveled somewhere else.

title: The dream
narration: In his dream, Pedro was in a strange place, with a forest, rocks, and clouds. Suddenly, the rocks and clouds began to change shape. They turned into animals, but not normal animals. He saw a donkey with butterfly wings. A rooster with the horns of a bull. A lion with the head of an eagle. And every single one of them was shouting the same mysterious word: "Alebrijes! Alebrijes! Alebrijes!" Louder... and louder... and louder!

title: From dream to art
narration: Then Pedro woke up. He had recovered! But he couldn't forget what he had seen. So he did what any artist would do: he grabbed his paper, paste, and paint, and he brought the creatures from his dream to life. He named them after the word they had shouted: alebrijes. Here's a fun fact: before Pedro, "alebrije" wasn't a word in Spanish, or in any other language. His dream invented it!

title: Famous fans
narration: At first, some people thought his creatures were a little too strange. But a few very famous artists loved them. The painters Diego Rivera and Frida Kahlo admired Pedro's work, and Rivera even asked him to make pieces for him. Little by little, Pedro's workshop became well known. His sons and grandchildren learned to make alebrijes too, and the Linares family still makes them today.

title: Alebrijes travel to Oaxaca
narration: In 1975, a filmmaker named Judith Bronowski made a documentary about Pedro Linares and brought him to the United States to show his art, alongside other Mexican artisans. One of them was Manuel Jiménez, a woodcarver from the village of San Antonio Arrazola, in the state of Oaxaca. Carvers in Oaxaca were already making animal figures from wood. Inspired by the bold colors and fantastic creatures of alebrijes, they gave the idea a whole new life.

title: Copal wood alebrijes
narration: Today, Oaxacan villages like San Martín Tilcajete and San Antonio Arrazola are famous for wooden alebrijes. Artisans carve them from the soft wood of the copal tree, using machetes and knives. Then the wood dries, and painters cover it with tiny dots, lines, and symbols. A single piece can take days, or even weeks, to finish! Some artists also add designs inspired by the Zapotec culture, one of the Indigenous peoples of Oaxaca. So now there are two great alebrije traditions: paper and cardboard in Mexico City, and carved wood in Oaxaca.

title: Giant alebrijes!
narration: In 1990, Pedro Linares received Mexico's National Prize for Arts and Sciences, one of the country's highest honors. He passed away in 1992, but his creatures kept growing. Literally! Every year since 2007, Mexico City's Museum of Popular Art has organized a parade of monumental alebrijes, where teams build creatures several meters tall and march them through the streets.

title: Alebrijes in the movies
narration: And you may have already met an alebrije without knowing it. In the 2017 movie Coco, the giant winged jaguar Pepita and the dog Dante become glowing alebrijes. In the movie, alebrijes are spirit guides in the Land of the Dead. That was a creative idea from the filmmakers. The real alebrijes came from one man's dream, not from an ancient legend. But the movie helped kids all over the world fall in love with them.

title: Quick quiz!
narration: Okay, let's see if you were paying attention! Pause the video and answer these three questions. Number one: who created the first alebrijes? Number two: what happened in 1936 that inspired them? Number three: in Oaxaca, what kind of wood are alebrijes carved from? ... Ready? The answers are: Pedro Linares, a fever dream, and copal wood!

title: Your turn!
narration: So here's your challenge. If you had a dream like Pedro's, what would your alebrije look like? Pick two or three animals, combine their best parts, and cover your creature with your boldest colors and patterns. Who knows? Your creature might become the next legend. Because sometimes, the best ideas come from our wildest dreams.
